column3: Direct parallel: seeing "the greatest" among the Lord's signs; it also leaves the signs as selected rather than exhaustive evidence.
A manifest messenger makes remembrance available; a secondary parallel to the sign being shown before Pharaoh.
Pairs false claims with arrogance toward signs and a humiliating outcome, extending the refusal that follows the showing.
Direct parallel: Moses is shown the greatest signs before his mission to Pharaoh, so seeing precedes his showing in 79:20.
Immediate continuation: Pharaoh answers the shown sign with denial and disobedience.
Pharaoh's unjust self-exaltation and denial of return clarify the disposition confronting the sign.
Direct later parallel: the "greatest" catastrophe follows the earlier greatest sign, preserving warning and eventual consequence together.
Immediate mission setting: Moses is sent to Pharaoh because he has overstepped.
The greatest seizure supplies a later, punitive scale of greatness alongside the corrective sign.
The greatest fire gives a remote consequence-side use of greatness, not an account of the sign itself.
Clear signs and guidance frame signs as disclosed direction, a secondary lens on why the sign is shown.
Great scheming is a contrary human use of magnitude: organized resistance rather than revealed evidence.
Close Pharaoh parallel: signs are shown in escalating magnitude, initially for return rather than immediate destruction.
Immediate narrative opening for the Moses account in which 79:20 occurs.
Calls the narrated outcome a sign while noting that most still do not believe, preserving visibility without compelled acceptance.
A seen sign can be met with collective mockery, a close parallel to Pharaoh's non-acceptance.
Immediate prior invitation: purification and awe are offered before the sign is shown.
Hearing signs followed by persistent arrogance shows that exposure to evidence need not become acceptance.
Links denial of signs with an arrogant claim of superior power; a close analogue to Pharaoh's response.
Moses brings clear proofs to Pharaoh and others, who then act arrogantly; direct narrative reinforcement.
Showing signs through benefit invites patient, grateful recognition; a receptive counterpoint to Pharaoh's refusal.
Uses greatness for grave warning, offering only a distant scale-and-consequence parallel.
Immediate narrative conclusion: the Pharaoh episode becomes a lesson for the one who fears.
The phrase "great error" reverses an accusation against warners, but has no close showing-of-signs link.
The greater punishment supplies a consequence-side use of comparative magnitude after turning away.
Immediate commissioning context: the Lord calls Moses before sending him to Pharaoh.
Arrogance produces refusal and disbelief; an archetypal parallel to rejecting a command or sign.
Explicit seeing at a clear horizon supplies a secondary model of manifest perception.
Direct Pharaoh parallel: when the signs arrive, the response is laughter rather than recognition.
Denial of signs is tied to enduring recompense; a consequence parallel, despite the auxiliary contrary branch.
States that signs are shown and asks which can be denied, directly joining display and responsibility.
Immediate continuation: Pharaoh gathers and calls out after the sign episode.
Small and great are both recorded; this is an accountability parallel, not a reading of the greatest sign.
Age, loss, and reflection on signs do not add a focused parallel to 79:20.
Immediate prior aim: Moses offers guidance toward the Lord and awe before the sign is shown.
The self-exalting group rejects what others believe; a social parallel to Pharaoh's resistant posture.
A vision functions as a test and can increase great overstepping, a secondary visibility-and-response parallel.
Public display without inward presence is a remote counterpoint to a genuinely shown sign.
Earthly arrogance and harmful plotting recoil on their authors; a secondary consequence for Pharaoh-like self-exaltation.
Command to magnify the Lord supplies a contrary scale to Pharaoh's later self-magnification.
Immediate continuation: Pharaoh turns away and strives after the encounter.
Arrogance is triggered by a monotheistic claim; it clarifies how a disclosed truth can meet status-protecting refusal.
The call to consider claimed deities is only a distant contrast between objects of sight and the Lord's signs.
Later visibility: the blaze is made manifest to whoever sees, echoing the narrative's movement from shown sign to seen outcome.
A person's striving will be seen, making visibility a later evaluative disclosure rather than self-managed display.
Demand for an even greater, open sight after clear proofs shows that more display does not ensure acceptance.
The true High and Great provides a contrary standard to Pharaoh's claim of height.
Refusal joined to self-exaltation gives the archetypal pattern of arrogance blocking obedience.
Performative visibility contrasts with a sign shown by God; the contrast is secondary rather than narrative.
Immediate continuation: Pharaoh answers with the false claim to be the highest lord.
Again names God as High and Great, supplying a theological counter-scale to Pharaoh's self-claim.
Comparative sin and benefit, though followed by clarification of signs, do not focus the showing in 79:20.
Non-arrogance is associated with openness, a contrary disposition to Pharaoh's response.
Signs will be shown and recognized, while deeds remain observed; close support for recognition without erasing accountability.
Greater concealed hostility and clear signs do not yield a focused connection to the Pharaoh scene.
Immediate finale: seeing the event compresses worldly duration, sustaining the later-unavoidable-sight reading.
Distinguishes claimed arrogance from genuine elevation, a secondary counterpoint to Pharaoh's self-ranking.
Those who speak falsely about God are visibly humiliated; self-exaltation ends in its reversal.
God's preparation of Moses supplies mission context, but is secondary to the showing in 79:20.
Turning away and self-exaltation form a close behavioural parallel to Pharaoh's post-sign response.
Denial of signs and arrogance away from them lead to abiding punishment; direct refusal-and-consequence parallel.
An avoided truth arrives inexorably at death, a remote anticipation of later unavoidable disclosure.
Great dominion and repeated seeing use the same broad motifs but do not illuminate Pharaoh's sign.
Seeing the consequence of deeds and a great favor is only a broad outcome parallel.
A journey is undertaken so that signs may be shown; it supports the purposeful-showing motif in a different setting.
Accumulated numbers and arrogance prove unable to protect; a social consequence parallel.
Even seeing every sign need not yield belief when arrogance reverses the choice of path; one of the closest interpretive parallels.
Ostentatious public departure and blocking the way give a secondary contrary pattern of display and obstruction.
Great divine favor is a remote use of magnitude, not evidence about 79:20's sign.
The largest visible celestial candidate still sets; it supplies a secondary test of sensory greatness against enduring authority.
Moses is sent with signs to Pharaoh and his council, directly situating 79:20 within the wider confrontation.
Creation as a sign offers a general evidence parallel with little Pharaoh-specific value.
The weight of refusal and desire for another sign show that a sign does not force inner response.
Followers discover that arrogant leaders cannot avert punishment; secondary aftermath of Pharaoh-like hierarchy.
What God shows grounds just judgment; a distant procedural use of showing rather than a sign confrontation.
Seeing a complete record, small and great, is a general accountability parallel to later disclosure.
The address "have you seen" begins a separate exposure of denial; only a remote perception motif.
Great corruption through alliances does not add a focused reading of 79:20.
Demanding to see the Lord is tied to great inward arrogance, clarifying a controlling rather than receptive demand for sight.
Uncovering and an inability to prostrate offer a distant later-disclosure and refusal parallel.
After being reminded by signs, turning away is condemned; close support for refusal after disclosure.
A witness accepts comparable evidence while others reject it arrogantly, preserving divergent responses to one proof.
What was denied becomes seen at close range, a future-visibility counterpart to the sign already shown in 79:20.
A local punishment points beyond itself to a greater one, retaining both warning and larger consequence.
The term for greatness describes an elderly father, with no focused connection to 79:20.
Patience, calling, and distress do not materially illuminate the showing of the greatest sign.
Rejecting service through arrogance ends in universal gathering; a secondary reversal of self-exaltation.
The weak blame the arrogant when punishment is seen, extending the social aftermath of arrogant leadership.
The call to consider a past divine act gives a remote model of recognition through reported evidence.
Differentiated cosmic signs support knowledge generally, but not the specific Pharaoh encounter.
The rhetorical question about the steep path has no focused connection to 79:20.
Great abhorrence for saying without doing is not a focused sign or Pharaoh parallel.
Demand for a sign is answered by warning and guidance, showing that a spectacular token is not the whole guidance role.
Disputants over signs have no escape; a secondary limit on argumentative evasion after evidence.
The gardens and springs passage does not add a focused reading of 79:20.
Destroyed settlements remain signs for those moving among them, turning historical aftermath into warning evidence.
Clear proofs can still be followed by divisive injustice, preserving non-compulsory response to evidence.
Persistent denial of God's signs is portrayed as being turned away, closely explaining a settled refusal.
Denial of signs and the meeting yields deeds without weight, a secondary reversal of claimed stature.
Denial of signs and the final meeting end in compulsory presence within punishment, extending the consequence trajectory.
Moses is sent with God's signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, directly establishing the mission and audience of 79:20.
Moses casts what is in his hand before Pharaoh, supplying one concrete constituent of the sign-display.
Moses brings forth his hand, visibly transformed for the onlookers; a second concrete constituent of the display.
Successive detailed signs are sent to Pharaoh's people, yet they remain arrogant; this extends 79:20 from display to persistent refusal.
Moses and Aaron are sent with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs; a close parallel to the narrative setting.
When the truth comes to Pharaoh's circle, it is reclassified as magic; this gives their interpretive response to shown evidence.
Fear under Pharaoh limits the response to Moses, showing how power conditions reception of the signs.
Pharaoh's body is left as a sign for those after him, extending the earlier sign encounter into historical aftermath.
Moses is sent with signs and clear authority to Pharaoh and his chiefs, directly paralleling 79:20's evidentiary mission.
Moses is given nine clear signs, and Pharaoh's response is explicitly recalled; this is a major parallel inventory for 79:20.
Moses addresses Pharaoh regarding the visible signs and his ruin, joining manifest evidence to Pharaoh's final outcome.
Moses and Aaron are commissioned to come to Pharaoh with a sign from their Lord, immediately framing the purpose of 79:20.
The closest verbal-narrative parallel: Pharaoh is shown all the signs, then denies and refuses.
Pharaoh answers the signs by charging Moses with magic and treating the encounter as a threat to his order.
The magicians respond to the displayed evidence by prostration, preserving a contrary reception to Pharaoh's denial.
Moses and Aaron are sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs with signs and manifest authority.
Pharaoh's chiefs meet the two messengers with arrogance, supplying the immediate resistant posture around the signs.
Moses offers a clear thing to Pharaoh in response to his challenge, directly opening the sign demonstration.
Moses casts his staff and it becomes a manifest serpent, a concrete sign relevant to 79:20.
Moses draws forth his hand for the observers, preserving the second visible sign in the Pharaoh confrontation.
Pharaoh's chiefs call the visible sign magic, a close parallel to rejection through re-description.
Moses' hand is named among nine signs sent to Pharaoh and his people, directly connecting a concrete sign to the target audience.
When the signs come visibly, Pharaoh's people call them manifest magic; this sharply preserves evidence and denial together.
They deny the signs despite inward certainty, through wrongdoing and arrogance; one of the closest readings of refusal after sight.
Staff and hand are given to Moses as two proofs for Pharaoh and his chiefs, specifying the evidence that 79:20 compresses.
When Moses brings clear signs to Pharaoh's circle, they call them invented magic, preserving the contrary reading of the display.
Moses is sent with signs and clear authority, explicitly naming Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun as recipients.
Those recipients answer the messenger with accusations of magic and falsehood, detailing resistance to the signs.
Pharaoh's people are tested through the coming of an honored messenger, giving a close episode-level parallel.
Signs containing a manifest test are given in the Moses narrative, supporting the trial dimension of what is shown.
Moses is sent to Pharaoh with clear authority, a concise direct parallel to the confrontation behind 79:20.
Pharaoh turns away in his power and labels Moses a magician or madman, extending the rejection that follows the display.
Pharaoh's people deny all the signs, directly generalizing the refusal begun after the greatest sign.
A messenger is sent to Pharaoh, providing a later concise recapitulation of the same commissioned confrontation.
Pharaoh disobeys the messenger and is seized, supplying the consequence trajectory after the sign is rejected.
